bull_thesis: The bull case is that a signed, regulator-gated asset sale closes inside the next ten weeks and the market finally marks the surviving business at something close to what a private buyer just paid. On 29 April 2026 FTAI Infrastructure agreed to sell Long Ridge Energy and Power, its 485-505 megawatt gas plant on the Ohio River, to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for roughly $1.52 billion. That price is about fourteen times the plant's annualised first-quarter earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation of $26.4 million. It is a hard, third-party mark, and it says the private market values these assets far above where the public shares trade. Closing does three concrete things. It wipes out about $1.16 billion of debt at the asset level. It funds roughly $291 to $300 million of repayment at the parent, cutting total debt from $3.814 billion to about $2.377 billion and saving around $30 million of interest every year. And it converts a five-asset conglomerate that nobody can value into a rail-and-terminals company that anyone can. The conditions list is short: antitrust clearance and a change-of-control approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, whose application was filed 8 May 2026 in docket EC26-92. Management guided on the first-quarter call to approval by the middle of the third quarter, with the chief executive saying there are no reasons the process should be prolonged. The buyer cleared its own financing obstacle in June 2026 by obtaining bondholder consents to amend Long Ridge's 8.75% notes due 2032. No financing contingency has been disclosed. What is left afterwards is genuinely good. The combined Transtar and Wheeling and Lake Erie railroads produced $40.2 million of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the first quarter, up 31% from a year earlier, with $23 million of annual cost savings identified ($10 million already taken) and more than $50 million of further integration upside named. Management points to a near-term annualised rail figure of $220 million or better. Jefferson, the Gulf Coast terminal, earned $14.4 million in the quarter against $8.0 million a year earlier, and management says it is pursuing three opportunities together worth more than $50 million of incremental annual earnings. Repauno's second phase reaches mechanical completion this autumn and starts operating in the first quarter of 2027. Management has said Jefferson and Repauno are themselves sale candidates over the next twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of expected excess cash aimed at parent debt. Sell-side coverage was initiated by Citizens on 15 July 2026 with a favourable rating and a $10 target, valuing the railroads at fourteen times, below the more than fifteen times at which comparable regional railroads have historically traded. Three analysts average about $11.67. And critically, the announcement on 30 April did not re-rate anything: the shares have fallen since, to $4.23 against a fifty-two-week high of $7.94, so the entry is at the low with the event still ahead. The conditions this case depends on: the energy regulator approves without material conditions or a long delay; the bulk of the proceeds actually goes to debt rather than acquisitions; and the rail run-rate arrives on schedule.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that this is a thinly capitalised stub with an event, and that the event, even if it closes, does not fix the capital structure. Start with what sits ahead of the common. As of 31 March 2026 there was $3.84 billion of debt, including a $1.315 billion parent term loan costing 9.75% and maturing in February 2028, a Repauno term loan of $108.3 million maturing 30 November 2026, and Jefferson bonds that were refinanced on 1 July 2026 into a $230 million bridge maturing 30 June 2027 at the benchmark rate plus 5.50% with step-ups. Behind that debt but ahead of the common sit two preferred instruments: a $1.0 billion preferred sold to funds managed by Ares Management, carried at $970.5 million with a redemption value of $1.4 billion, paying 10% for three years, then 12%, then 14%; and a Series B preferred carried at $152.6 million with a $192.0 million redemption value. Total equity is negative $303.1 million. The market value of the common is about $500 million. So roughly $4.9 billion of senior claims stand in front of a half-billion-dollar sliver. Two structural details make it worse and are widely missed. The Ares preferred was issued by the rail holding company, not by the parent, so on the railroads, the asset management calls the future, the parent's claim ranks behind it. And Ares also holds warrants over up to 20% of that rail holding company's common units (172,500 units at $857.748, expiring 25 August 2035), so the parent's economic share of the best business can fall toward 80%. Any valuation of the railroads that forgets these is overstating what reaches the shareholder by roughly a fifth of the rail stub plus a billion dollars of preferred. Now the operating picture. First-quarter 2026 revenue nearly doubled to $188.4 million but the company lost $127.2 million, or $1.32 per share against a consensus expectation near $0.35, on $82.5 million of quarterly interest and a $45.9 million loss on extinguishing debt. Cash from operations was negative $69.4 million. The filing's statement that liquidity is sufficient is expressly conditioned on the Long Ridge sale being completed. Strip the sale out and that sentence stops working. On the event itself: no approval order has issued in docket EC26-92 as of today, and on 29 May 2026 the independent market monitor for the PJM grid formally asked the regulator to approve the sale only if the buyer commits to keeping the plant's output in PJM's markets. A bitcoin and data-centre operator buying a power plant has every reason to take that power behind the meter, which is precisely why the objection was filed. It is unlikely to kill the deal; it is a very plausible way for the middle of the third quarter to become the fourth. The buyer and the seller do not even publish the same window: MARA says the second half of 2026, the seller says the third quarter. Finally, closing is a smaller event than it sounds. Roughly $300 million of parent repayment against $1.31 billion of parent debt still leaves about $2.377 billion of total debt and the entire preferred stack intact, and management has said part of the residual proceeds may fund acquisitions rather than debt reduction, which for a company at this leverage is the wrong instinct. What confirms the bear: an approval order that slips past the third quarter or attaches operating conditions; second-quarter results on 5 August that push the closing window out; another quarter of negative operating cash flow; or proceeds redirected to acquisitions.
sop_bull: Event wins and the surviving assets are marked near private-market value. Railroads: $240 million of annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (management's $220 million-plus near-term figure plus part of the more than $50 million of identified integration upside) at 15 times, in line with where comparable regional railroads have historically traded, gives $3.60 billion. Jefferson: $80 million annualised, reflecting the three named opportunities landing, at 11 times gives $0.88 billion. Repauno: $0.45 billion, crediting phase two coming online in early 2027 at roughly capital invested. Residual cash retained from the sale after debt repayment: $0.06 billion. Gross value $4.99 billion. Deduct pro-forma total debt after closing of $2.377 billion (management's own bridge from $3.814 billion), the Ares rail preferred at its $0.97 billion carrying value, and the Series B preferred at $0.15 billion, then allow roughly $0.15 billion for the dilution from the Ares warrants over up to 20% of the rail holding company. Equity value about $1.34 billion on 118.2 million shares, or roughly $11.50 per share, with a stretch to $13.00 if the terminals are actually sold at anything like the fourteen times the power plant just fetched. This sits at the top of the published street range of $10.00 to $13.00.
sop_bear: The event fails or slips indefinitely and the stub is repriced for refinancing stress. Railroads: $200 million at 11 times gives $2.20 billion. Jefferson: $56 million at 8 times gives $0.45 billion. Repauno, unfinished and not yet earning, $0.15 billion. Gross value $2.80 billion. Deduct debt that never gets reduced and stays at $3.84 billion, and the equity is underwater before the $1.12 billion of preferred is even reached. On that arithmetic the residual claim is nominally zero. In practice a levered stub with an intact franchise does not trade to zero while the railroads still earn, so the observable floor is behavioural rather than asset-backed: with the parent term loan still costing 9.75%, the Jefferson bridge due June 2027 needing to be termed out again, the Repauno loan due November 2026, negative operating cash flow, and the liquidity statement in the filings expressly resting on the sale, a deal-break realistically prices the shares at $2.50 to $3.00. Call the floor $2.75. Note plainly that the $3.90 level carried in the source entry is the fifty-two-week low, a chart level, and nothing on the balance sheet supports it as a recovery value: book equity is already negative $303.1 million, there is no net cash, and the common has no contractual payout in any scenario.
sop_fair_value: $6.50 per share, within a range of $5.00 to $9.00
sop_breakdown: Base case, valued after the Long Ridge sale closes. Railroads (Transtar plus Wheeling and Lake Erie): $235 million of annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at 14 times, the multiple the newly initiating sell-side analyst uses and below the historical regional-rail range, gives $3.29 billion. Jefferson terminal: $75 million at 11 times gives $0.83 billion. Repauno: $0.45 billion, discounted for the fact that phase two does not operate until early 2027. Residual cash from the sale: $0.06 billion. Gross value $4.63 billion. Less pro-forma total debt of $2.377 billion, less the Ares rail preferred at its $0.97 billion carrying value, less the Series B preferred at $0.15 billion, less roughly $0.15 billion for the Ares warrants over up to 20% of the rail holding company. Equity value about $0.98 billion on 118.2 million shares, or $8.29 per share on those inputs. Because the answer is extremely sensitive to the rail multiple and the rail run-rate, the base case is set below that at $6.50 to reflect execution risk on the $220 million-plus run-rate, the unfinished Repauno build, and the possibility that proceeds are partly spent on acquisitions rather than debt. Two useful sensitivities: every one turn on the rail multiple is worth about $1.86 per share, and every $10 million of rail earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation is worth about $1.18 per share at 14 times. That is why the published street range spans $10.00 to $13.00 while a stricter treatment of the preferred and the warrants lands nearer $5.00 to $6.00.
risk_reward: About 3.2 to 1 measured to the event-resolved target, and about 1.5 to 1 measured to the base-case fair value. From $4.23, the upside to a $9.00 event-resolved target is +113% and the downside to a realistic $2.75 deal-break price is -35%. Against the $6.50 base-case fair value the upside is +54% against the same -35% downside. This corrects the risk-reward of 18.6 to 1 carried in the source entry, which was computed against a $3.90 floor. That $3.90 is the fifty-two-week low, not an asset value, and using it understates the loss side by roughly a factor of five. The asymmetry here is real but ordinary, not extreme.
catalyst_status_note: Definitive equity purchase agreement signed 29 April 2026 and announced 30 April 2026: MARA USA Corporation to acquire 100% of Long Ridge Energy and Power from FTAI Infrastructure subsidiaries for a base price of about $1.52 billion plus assumption of Long Ridge debt. Advisers Jefferies and Lazard; counsel Skadden, Arps. Conditions are antitrust clearance and change-of-control approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission; no financing contingency disclosed. The regulatory application was filed 8 May 2026 in docket EC26-92, with a comment deadline of 29 May 2026; no final order granting authorisation has issued as of 27 July 2026. In early June 2026 the buyer completed a consent solicitation and obtained bondholder approvals to amend Long Ridge's 8.75% notes due 2032, clearing a financing obstacle on its side. On the first-quarter call the chief executive guided to regulatory approval by the middle of the third quarter and said there are no reasons the process should be prolonged. Two qualifications on the date: the seller guides to a third-quarter close while the buyer guides to the second half of 2026, and neither has published a contractual outside date, so 30 September 2026 is a guided quarter-end rather than a binding deadline. The event has not fired and the shares have fallen since the announcement, so no part of the re-rating has been spent.
catalyst_summary: A signed $1.52 billion sale of the Long Ridge power plant to MARA, awaiting only a change-of-control approval from the energy regulator, guided to close by the end of the third quarter of 2026 and cutting total debt from $3.8 billion to $2.4 billion; the shares at $4.23 sit near their fifty-two-week low against a $9.00 event-resolved value and a realistic $2.75 deal-break price.
dated_milestone: Change-of-control approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, application filed 8 May 2026 in docket EC26-92, guided by management to arrive in the middle of the third quarter of 2026, with the sale closing by 30 September 2026 on the seller's guidance. Nearest scheduled checkpoint: second-quarter 2026 results after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, with the conference call at 8:00 a.m. Eastern on Thursday 6 August 2026.
forcing_function: The approval order in docket EC26-92 is the trigger. Once the energy regulator signs off, the sale closes within days, and closing is self-executing: about $1.16 billion of debt at the asset level disappears with the business, roughly $291 to $300 million of parent debt is repaid, total debt falls from $3.814 billion to about $2.377 billion, and about $30 million a year of interest expense goes away. That is a mechanical change to the capital structure that no analyst has to be persuaded of. Two secondary forcing events follow inside twelve months. The first is the second-quarter report on 5 August 2026, which is where any change in the closing window will be disclosed and which is the nearest dated risk in either direction. The second is the sale of the Jefferson and Repauno terminals, which management has said are candidates over the next twelve to eighteen months with roughly $700 million of excess cash earmarked to cut parent debt further; the fourteen times multiple the power plant just fetched is the reference price for those. The deeper forcing function is arithmetic: once the conglomerate is reduced to railroads earning $220 million or more, the business becomes straightforwardly comparable to publicly traded regional railroads, and the discount that exists because nobody can model five unrelated assets at once stops being defensible.
consensus_delta: The market is treating this as a distressed balance sheet with a story attached, and is pricing the balance sheet while ignoring the mark. Three specific street assumptions look wrong. First, the shares have fallen since 30 April, when the sale was announced, from the mid-fives to $4.23, which means the market has assigned essentially no value to a signed, advised, financing-unconditional agreement with a single substantive approval outstanding. That is not scepticism about the deal; it is inattention to it, in a $500 million company that three analysts follow. Second, the market is anchoring on the reported loss rather than the transaction price. First-quarter loss per share of $1.32 against an expected $0.35 dominated the headlines, and the $82.5 million of quarterly interest and $45.9 million loss on extinguishing debt that caused it are the direct, one-time cost of the refinancing that makes the deleveraging possible. Third, and most concretely: the buyer is paying about fourteen times annualised earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for a merchant gas plant that had a planned outage in the quarter. If a power plant clears fourteen times in a private sale, the terminals and railroads are not worth the mid-single-digit implied multiple the public stub carries. Where we would part company with the bulls, however, is on how far this goes. The published street range of $10.00 to $13.00 appears to give little or no deduction for the $1.0 billion preferred sitting inside the rail holding company and the warrants over up to 20% of that entity, both of which rank ahead of the shareholder on the very asset the bull case is built on. Our disagreement with the market is therefore two-sided: the market is too pessimistic on the event and the private marks, and the sell-side is too generous on what actually reaches the common.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months contain more dated risk than the catalyst window suggests. The nearest is 5 August 2026, when second-quarter results land: another quarter of heavy interest expense is certain, another negative operating cash flow quarter is likely after the negative $69.4 million printed in the first quarter, and this is the venue where a slip in the closing window would be disclosed. The regulatory path is the second hazard. No order has issued in docket EC26-92, and the PJM market monitor's 29 May filing asks for conditions on the approval. Conditions are more likely than refusal, but conditions take time to negotiate and the middle of the third quarter can become the fourth quarter without anything actually going wrong. Note also that the buyer publishes a wider window than the seller. Third, the maturity ladder does not wait. The Repauno term loan of $108.3 million matures 30 November 2026. The Jefferson bridge taken on 1 July 2026 matures 30 June 2027 and carries the benchmark rate plus 5.50% with step-ups, minimum liquidity of $20 million, and mandatory prepayment from excess cash flow; it is a bridge to a permanent financing that has not been arranged. Fourth, the liquidity language in the first-quarter filing states that management's planned actions, including the sale of Long Ridge, are considered probable and sufficient to meet obligations over the next twelve months. That is a sentence with a load-bearing conditional in it. If the sale slips past the year-end, auditors and lenders will revisit it, and that is the mechanism by which a timing problem becomes a solvency conversation. Fifth, Repauno's phase two reaches mechanical completion this autumn and does not begin operating until the first quarter of 2027, so it consumes cash for two more quarters before it contributes any. The window between now and closing is where this position can lose a third of its value without the thesis being wrong.
positioning_washout: The forced selling has largely already happened, which is the constructive part of the setup. This was spun out of an aviation leasing company in 2022 and initially attracted an income-oriented, infrastructure-yield shareholder base. That base has been given every reason to leave: the dividend was eliminated, the balance sheet levered up, book equity is now negative $303.1 million, and the shares have fallen from a fifty-two-week high of $7.94 to $4.23, a decline of nearly half, with the fifty-day average at $4.51 and the two-hundred-day at $5.10, so the trend has been persistently downward rather than a single shock. At about a $500 million market value the company has fallen out of the size band where most institutional infrastructure and income mandates can hold it, and index membership at the small-cap end brings mechanical selling on rebalancing rather than support. The first-quarter miss of $1.32 against $0.35 was the kind of print that flushes the last of the quality-screen holders, and the shares traded down about 7.4% after hours on it. What that leaves is a thin, event-oriented holder base near the fifty-two-week low with a signed transaction pending, which is the composition you want going into a catalyst: the sellers who had to sell have sold, and the marginal buyer is now someone underwriting the event rather than the yield. The offsetting risk is liquidity itself: roughly 785,000 shares traded in the most recent session on a $500 million market value, so the same thinness that produced the overshoot down will produce a violent move on any adverse headline, and there is no natural long-term holder to absorb it.
moderator_conclusion: Buy it now, and size it as a levered stub with a live event rather than as an arbitrage with a floor. The event is genuine. A definitive agreement was signed on 29 April 2026 to sell the Long Ridge power plant to MARA for about $1.52 billion, the regulatory application was filed on 8 May in docket EC26-92, the buyer cleared its bondholder consents in June, no financing contingency exists, and management has guided to approval by the middle of the third quarter. Nothing about it has fired, and the shares have actually fallen since the announcement, so none of the re-rating has been spent. At $4.23, close to the fifty-two-week low of $3.90 and against a high of $7.94, you are being paid to wait for a transaction that reduces total debt from $3.8 billion to $2.4 billion and saves about $30 million of interest a year, on a company whose surviving railroads grew earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation 31% year over year. There is no wash-out worth waiting for; this is the wash-out. Two things keep this from being the maximum-conviction version of this setup. The first is the floor. The entry carried into this review assumes $3.90 of downside protection, and that number is a chart level, not a recovery value. Book equity is negative $303.1 million, there is no net cash, operating cash flow was negative $69.4 million last quarter, and the filing's own liquidity assurance is expressly conditioned on this sale closing. A deal-break realistically prices the shares at $2.50 to $3.00, which turns a claimed reward-to-risk of roughly 18 to 1 into about 3 to 1. That is still an attractive trade; it is not a defined-risk one, and the difference matters for sizing. The second is the capital structure that survives the sale. A $1.0 billion preferred, carried at $970.5 million with a $1.4 billion redemption value and paying 10% rising to 14%, sits inside the rail holding company, ahead of the parent's claim on the very asset the bull case rests on, and the same holder has warrants over up to 20% of that entity's common units. Value the railroads at fourteen times and forget those two items and you get the street's $10.00 to $13.00; remember them and you get closer to $6.50. Our base case is $6.50 with a range of $5.00 to $9.00, and the $9.00 end requires not just the sale closing but the rail run-rate arriving and the terminals being monetised near the multiple the power plant just fetched. Watch 5 August, when second-quarter results are reported, for any change in the closing window, and watch docket EC26-92 for the approval order and for whether the market monitor's requested conditions are attached. Enter now, keep the position modest, and treat a slip of the window past the third quarter as a reason to reassess rather than to add.
interrogator_dossier:
# FTAI Infrastructure Inc. (FIP) — Event Dossier

*Prepared 27 July 2026. This is an event-driven special situation, not a quality or compounding case. The question is whether a signed, regulator-gated asset sale closes inside the window, what the shares are worth once it does, and what actually catches the stock if it does not.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

FTAI Infrastructure was spun out of FTAI Aviation in August 2022 as a collection of five hard-asset businesses: two freight railroads, two river terminals, and a gas-fired power plant. The story it told at the spin was a build-out story — spend capital now, harvest later.

The story today is the opposite, and the turn happened fast. Over the past twelve months management has pivoted from assembling assets to selling them and paying down debt:

- **August 2025** — agreed to buy The Wheeling Corporation, owner of the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway (a Class II regional railroad with more than 1,000 miles of track across Ohio, Pennsylvania, West Virginia and Maryland), for $1.05 billion in cash. To fund it the company raised $2.25 billion: roughly $1.25 billion of new debt at the parent and $1.0 billion of preferred equity sold to funds managed by Ares Management, issued not at the parent but inside the rail holding company. The deal closed 25 August 2025.
- **30 April 2026** — agreed to sell Long Ridge Energy & Power (a 485–505 megawatt combined-cycle gas plant at Hannibal, Ohio, working interests in gas wells, and roughly 1,600 acres on the Ohio River) to a subsidiary of MARA Holdings for about $1.52 billion, before closing adjustments.
- **1 July 2026** — refinanced $217.9 million of Jefferson terminal bonds with a $230 million secured bridge loan from Jefferies Finance, maturing 30 June 2027.
- **Stated next step** — Jefferson and Repauno are described as sale candidates over the next twelve to eighteen months, with roughly $700 million of expected excess cash earmarked to cut parent-level debt further.

So the arc is: conglomerate assembled, conglomerate now being taken apart, with freight rail as the intended survivor. That is a genuine change of direction, and it is the reason the shares are worth analysing at all.

---

## 2. THE EVENT: IS IT REAL, DATED, AND BINDING?

**Real.** Yes. This is a signed definitive agreement, not a process or an exploration. MARA USA Corporation entered an equity purchase agreement on 29 April 2026 to acquire 100% of Long Ridge Energy & Power from FTAI Infrastructure subsidiaries for a base price of approximately $1.5 billion plus assumption of Long Ridge's existing debt. Both sides announced it the following morning. Jefferies and Lazard advised the seller; Skadden, Arps was seller's counsel.

**Binding, with a short conditions list.** The announced conditions are clearance under the Hart-Scott-Rodino antitrust waiting period, approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for the change of control of the power plant, and customary closing conditions. On the first-quarter call management was unusually plain about how narrow the gate is: chief executive Ken Nicholson said the energy regulator "needs to approve the change of control" and that there are "no reasons why it should be a prolonged process." No financing contingency has been disclosed — MARA is not conditioning the purchase on raising money.

**Dated — but by guidance, not by contract.** This is the single most important qualification in the file, and the two sides do not say the same thing:

| Source | Stated timing |
|---|---|
| FTAI Infrastructure, 30 April 2026 release and first-quarter call | Close in the **third quarter of 2026**; regulatory approval expected **"mid-third quarter"** |
| MARA Holdings, same transaction | Close in the **second half of 2026** |

A seller guiding to one quarter and a buyer guiding to a half-year is not a contradiction, but it is a gap, and the looser of the two is the one that governs how patient the buyer has to be. The 30 September date this candidate carries is the seller's guided quarter-end, not a contractual drop-dead date that anyone has published.

**Where the approval actually stands.** The application under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act was filed with the energy regulator on 8 May 2026 in docket EC26-92, with a comment deadline of 29 May 2026. As of today no final order granting authorisation has surfaced in that docket. Two dated developments since:

- **29 May 2026** — the independent market monitor for the PJM grid filed comments urging the regulator to approve the sale only on condition that the buyer commit to keeping the plant's output in PJM's markets. The concern is obvious: a bitcoin and data-centre operator buying a power plant has every incentive to take that power behind the meter and out of the grid. This is a live conditioning risk. It is more likely to attach conditions or add weeks than to kill the deal, but it is exactly the kind of intervention that turns "mid-third quarter" into "fourth quarter."
- **Early June 2026** — MARA completed a consent solicitation and obtained the necessary bondholder approvals to amend Long Ridge Energy's 8.75% notes due 2032. That removes a financing obstacle on the buyer's side and is a meaningful, dated piece of progress.

**Verdict on the event: a hard, dated catalyst (a firm, scheduled event) that has not yet fired.** The agreement is signed, the regulatory clock is running, the buyer has cleared its own financing hurdle, and the seller has guided to a close inside the window. What it is not is contractually date-certain, and the guided window is the tighter of two published views.

**Next scheduled checkpoint:** second-quarter results after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, with the call the following morning. That is nine days away and is where any slippage will be disclosed.

---

## 3. CREDIBILITY OF THE SPONSOR

Management is Fortress-affiliated, led by Ken Nicholson. The record cuts both ways and the split is important.

**On transactions they deliver.** They said they would buy the Wheeling railroad and they closed it. They said they would raise $2.25 billion to fund it and they raised it. They said they would sell Long Ridge and they signed it — at roughly fourteen times the plant's annualised first-quarter earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, which is a strong price for a merchant gas plant and a genuine validation that private buyers pay far more for these assets than the public market does. They said they would refinance the Jefferson bonds and they did, on 1 July.

**On the profit and loss statement they do not.** First-quarter 2026 loss per share was $1.32 against a consensus expectation of about $0.35 — a miss of nearly four times. Revenue nearly doubled to $188.4 million, but the company still lost $127.2 million, driven by $82.5 million of quarterly interest expense and a $45.9 million loss on extinguishing debt during the refinancing. Cash from operations was negative $69.4 million in the quarter. Consolidated adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation were $70.6 million, which management notes would have topped $80 million but for a planned outage at Long Ridge — a fair adjustment, but it also means the reported number and the number management wants you to use have diverged for several quarters running.

**The pattern to name.** Every financing has been done at a price that protects the lender or the preferred holder and leaves the common shareholder with the residual risk: a 9.75% parent term loan, a bridge at the benchmark rate plus 5.50% with a step-up, and a $1.0 billion preferred that pays 10% for three years, 12% in years four through six, and 14% thereafter. Management has been reliable about *getting deals done* and unreliable about *what those deals cost the equity*. Score the deal execution high and the capital-structure stewardship low.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — WHAT ACTUALLY BACKSTOPS THE PRICE

This is where this candidate's own file needs correcting.

The floor carried in the watch entry is $3.90. That is the fifty-two-week low, a chart level. It is not an asset-backed recovery value, and nothing in the filings supports it as one. Here is what the balance sheet actually says as of 31 March 2026:

| Claim | Amount | Where it sits |
|---|---|---|
| Total debt | $3.84 billion | Parent term loan $1.315bn at 9.75% due Feb 2028; Long Ridge facilities and notes; Jefferson bonds; Repauno term loan $108m due Nov 2026 |
| Preferred sold to Ares | Carrying $970.5 million, redemption value $1.4 billion | Inside the **rail** holding company, ahead of the parent's claim on the crown jewel |
| Series B preferred | Carrying $152.6 million, redemption value $192.0 million | Parent |
| Total equity | **Negative $303.1 million** | — |
| Common shares outstanding | 118.2 million (6 May 2026) | Market value about $500 million at $4.23 |

Three things follow.

**First, the common stock is a thin slice at the bottom of a very tall stack.** Roughly $3.8 billion of debt and about $1.1 billion of preferred sit ahead of a $500 million equity market value. Book equity is already negative. There is no cash pile, no net-cash floor, and no contractual payout to the common in any scenario.

**Second, the Ares preferred is structurally senior to the parent on the best asset.** It was issued by the rail holding company, not by FTAI Infrastructure. So on the railroads — the business management says is the future — the parent's claim ranks behind a $1.0 billion instrument that compounds at 10% and steps to 12% and then 14%. Holders can demand redemption after the seventh anniversary (25 August 2032) and, if not redeemed within 120 days, can force a sale of the company. That is a long fuse, but it is a fuse.

**Third, and least discussed: Ares also holds warrants over up to 20% of the rail holding company's common units** (172,500 units at an exercise price of $857.748, exercisable on the earlier of the fifth anniversary or full repayment of the permanent debt financing, expiring 25 August 2035). So the parent's economic share of the railroads can fall toward 80%. Any sum-of-the-parts that values the rail business and forgets this is overstating what reaches the common by roughly a fifth of the rail stub.

**What the real floor looks like.** If the sale to MARA breaks or slips indefinitely, the following are simultaneously true: parent debt stays at $1.31 billion costing 9.75%; the $30 million a year of interest saving does not arrive; the Jefferson bridge still matures 30 June 2027 and has to be termed out again; the Repauno term loan matures 30 November 2026; operating cash flow is negative; and the language in the filings that liquidity is sufficient rests explicitly on the sale happening — management states that its planned actions, "including the sale of Long Ridge," are considered probable and sufficient to meet obligations over the next twelve months. Strip the sale out of that sentence and the sentence stops working.

A deal-break therefore is not a $3.90 event. A reasonable break price is **$2.50 to $3.00**, and that is a judgement about where a levered stub trades under refinancing stress, not a value anyone can point to on a balance sheet. The honest statement is that this position has a *defined catalyst* but **not** a *defined-risk floor*. Anyone sizing it as though $3.90 catches the fall is mis-measuring the trade by a wide margin.

---

## 5. CONCERNS AND POSITIVES

**Concerns**

- The stated floor is a chart level, not an asset value. Recovery risk-reward computed off it is inflated several-fold.
- Book equity is negative $303.1 million and operating cash flow was negative $69.4 million in the first quarter of 2026.
- The going-concern-adjacent language in the first-quarter filing is expressly conditioned on the Long Ridge sale closing.
- The energy regulator has not issued its order, and the PJM market monitor has formally asked for conditions on it (29 May 2026).
- Buyer and seller publish different closing windows — a half-year versus a quarter.
- The Ares preferred and its 20% rail warrant sit between the common and the best asset, and the preferred accretes at 10% rising to 14%.
- The Jefferson refinancing on 1 July was a bridge to June 2027, not a permanent solution — the same problem returns in eleven months.
- Management has said part of the proceeds may fund acquisitions rather than debt reduction. For a company at this leverage, that is the wrong instinct and the market has treated it as such.
- The shares are down from a fifty-two-week high of $7.94 to $4.23 and have kept falling *since* the sale was announced on 30 April. The announcement did not re-rate anything.

**Positives**

- The sale is signed, priced, and advised, with a narrow conditions list and no disclosed financing contingency.
- The price paid — about $1.52 billion for a business generating $26.4 million of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the first quarter — implies roughly fourteen times annualised. That is a hard, third-party mark showing private buyers value these assets far above where the public stub trades.
- The buyer has already cleared its bondholder consents (June 2026), removing a financing obstacle.
- The transaction removes about $1.16 billion of asset-level debt and funds roughly $291–300 million of parent debt repayment, cutting total debt from $3.814 billion to about $2.377 billion and saving roughly $30 million a year in interest.
- The surviving business is genuinely good. Rail adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation grew 31% year over year to $40.2 million in the first quarter, with $23 million of identified annual cost savings ($10 million already taken) and more than $50 million of further integration upside identified.
- Selling the power plant removes the most volatile and most capital-hungry piece of the portfolio and sharpens the company into a rail-and-terminals story that is far easier to value.
- Sell-side coverage was initiated by Citizens on 15 July 2026 with a favourable rating and a $10 target, using a fourteen times rail multiple — deliberately below the fifteen times and above at which comparable regional railroads have historically traded.

---

## 6. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Financing at the subsidiary, not the parent.** Both the big 2025 raise (rail holding company preferred) and the 2026 Jefferson bridge were done one level down. That preserves parent optionality but it also means each asset is progressively encumbered before the parent's claim attaches. Watch whether the next terminal financing follows the same pattern.
- **The vocabulary changed.** A year ago the language was growth, build-out, and phases. On the first-quarter 2026 call it is deleveraging, cost savings, run-rate, and monetisation. That shift is real and it usually precedes either a successful simplification or a forced one.
- **Management would not put a leverage target on the record.** Asked about it, they spoke about metrics continuing to improve rather than naming a number. For a company whose entire equity story is a deleveraging story, declining to name the destination is notable.
- **Nobody asked about the Ares preferred on the call and management did not raise it.** The single largest claim standing between the common shareholder and the railroads went undiscussed. That silence is itself information about how the market is modelling this name.

---

## 7. WHAT THE DIRECTOR MUST WEIGH

The trade is honest about itself if you state it plainly: **a signed, regulator-gated asset sale expected to close inside the next ten weeks, on a stock sitting near its fifty-two-week low, where the catalyst is credible but the floor is not.**

The upside case does not depend on the sale alone. Closing removes about $1.4 billion of debt and $30 million of annual interest, but it does not by itself take a $4.23 stock to $9. What takes it there is closing *plus* the rail business hitting its $220 million-plus run-rate and the terminals being monetised at anything near the multiple the power plant just fetched. The sale matters most as proof that the private mark is real.

The single thing to weigh before sizing: **this is not defined-risk.** The catalyst is dated and live, which is the reason to own it. But the loss is not bounded by anything you can verify. Size it as a levered stub with an event, not as an arbitrage with a floor.

On the conventional questions this candidate is deliberately not built to answer: the surviving franchise — regional freight rail with captive industrial shippers, irreplaceable track, and regulatory barriers to entry — is a narrow but real competitive advantage, and it is stable rather than eroding. There is no structural force threatening its terminal value; if anything, selling the merchant power plant removes the portfolio's most exposed piece. But none of that is the thesis. The thesis is the event.
